title: Starting a Small Corporation
summary: Choose the route → File the articles → Build the folder → Mark the deadlines
subtitle: Build a company folder that helps you start with clear ownership and fewer loose ends.

blocks.text: A company certificate can feel like the finish line. It is the start of a company that needs its own records and its own way to handle money. The website may cheer with a receipt, but your folder still has work to do.
Give your start a clear shape.
blocks.detail: You can turn a pile of forms into a company folder where every page has a job, so a client, bank or accountant gets answers fast.
blocks.extra: Section 05 walks you through that folder, one section at a time.

sections.title: Meet the company you are creating

blocks.text: A corporation is a separate legal person. It can own things and sign contracts in its own name. Registering a business name on its own does not create one.

People own pieces of the company called shares. Those owners are shareholders. Directors oversee the company, and officers run the daily work. In a small company, one person may hold all three roles, but each role still matters.

This lesson follows the paperwork after you decide to incorporate. It does not promise tax savings or remove every personal risk. Get a lawyer or accountant for choices that affect who owns what or how much tax you pay.

sections.title: Prepare the decisions behind the filing

blocks.text: You can incorporate federally with Corporations Canada, or under the rules of one province or territory. Think about where you will do business and which yearly filings each route brings. Check today’s fees on the official site before you commit, not an old screenshot.

Corporations Canada lets you pick a word name or take a numbered name, such as 1234567 Canada Inc. A numbered company can trade under a different name if that name is registered where the rules require it. Put the legal name on your contracts and invoices so clients know who they are dealing with.

Write down where you are incorporating before you open the form. Federal and provincial companies follow different routes. A federal company may still need to register in each province where it does business.

The main filing, called the articles of incorporation, sets up how the company is built. Share classes can carry different rights, such as votes or dividends. If two people will own the company, ask a lawyer about ownership and a shareholder agreement before you pick a template.

Get the registered office and first director details ready using your registry’s guide. Official mail goes to the registered office, so pick an address that meets the rules and that someone checks. Find out which details become public before you file.
A partner’s friendly promise is not a share record. Agree on who owns what before you file. Then record the shares the company issued and the money paid for them.

items.title: “Once the certificate arrives, the corporation is fully organised.”
items.text: Corporations Canada says setting up the company comes next. It still needs decisions about officers, banking and issuing shares, with the right records for each.

blocks.text: Keep the certificate and the filed articles together. Check the legal name and the date of incorporation against the confirmation. Keep your filing login safe, and give any helper their own access instead of sharing yours.
Federal costs and deadlines at a glance

items.title: FILING FEE
items.text: Incorporating online with Corporations Canada costs $200. The name search is built into the online form. Provincial fees and steps differ, so check your registry.

items.title: ANNUAL RETURN
items.text: File it each year within 60 days after the anniversary of your incorporation date. It costs $12 online. Federal companies file their significant-control details at the same time.

items.title: MISS IT AND LOSE IT
items.text: Corporations Canada can dissolve a company that stops filing annual returns. A calendar reminder is cheaper than starting over.

items.title: CORPORATE TAX
items.text: The T2 return is due six months after the tax year ends. Any tax owing is due sooner: two months after year-end, or three months for many small Canadian-controlled private companies.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: Priya’s nearly empty folder

blocks.text: Priya’s nearly empty folder
paragraphs: Priya ran a translation service in Calgary. She wanted her new company ready for its first business client. She made a folder called Company Start and pictured neat contracts beside the certificate. Staying organized mattered, because she worked evenings around family life.

Right after she incorporated federally, a client sent her a supplier form. It asked for the legal company name and the company’s bank details. Her folder held one certificate. Her draft invoice still used her old service name. And she had not decided how the company would use her personal laptop.

Priya opened more tabs and found three different task lists. She almost copied a share template from an online forum. Instead, she booked a short meeting with a lawyer. She also asked an accountant to check the money setup before she sent the form back.

With their help, she made the company decisions and filled in the share records. She opened a company bank account and changed the client agreement to name the company. Her folder now had labelled sections and a note beside each unfinished task.

Then the client asked her to add a second translator before work began. Priya had assumed that person would become a co-owner. But they wanted a paid role on the project, not shares. She paused the ownership talk and set up a simple service agreement instead.

The project started later than she had hoped. Still, everyone knew who was doing the work and who would be paid. At her next review, Priya found each document without opening ten tabs. Company Start finally held a real start.

blocks.text: Priya’s story is made up. Her smart move was to pause an unclear deal before signing, then get help with the papers that mattered.
A folder can give you breathing room.
blocks.detail: Clear company records let you answer a client’s questions in minutes, without rebuilding your decisions from memory.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows you what goes in each part of the folder.

blocks.text: This folder is a practice tool, not an official filing schedule. Give each section a status: ready, waiting or needs advice. Add who is responsible and a review date for every open item.

items.title: Formation: save the certificate, the filed articles and the registry receipts. Note where the company was formed.

Ownership and decisions: keep the by-laws, first resolutions, officer appointments and share records. Corporations Canada says a federal company can issue shares only once they are fully paid and the directors have approved it in writing.
Money: open the company bank account and set up bookkeeping. Keep receipts from the first purchase. Ask an accountant how to record money you put into the company.
Operations: put contracts and insurance in the company’s name. List the equipment and agreements you already have and get advice on moving them. Incorporating does not move them for you.

blocks.text: The CRA says a federal company gets a business number and a corporate income tax account when it is approved. Check the confirmation. GST/HST and payroll accounts are separate. Do not assume every tax account is open.

Add a section for permits before you serve clients. Alberta, for example, requires companies formed elsewhere, including federal ones, to register there. Check the rules in every province where you do business, and ask your city about local licences.

Most private federal companies must keep a register of individuals with significant control (ISC), meaning the people who own or control a large share. Corporations Canada requires you to file this at incorporation, with each annual return and within 15 days of any change to the register. Keep the full internal record safe.

items.title: “Incorporation makes insurance and contract review unnecessary.”
items.text: A personal guarantee can still put your own money at risk, and directors have legal duties. Read the actual agreement and insurance before you sign.

blocks.text: By day 90, review the folder and your calendar. The yearly return to Corporations Canada is separate from the T2 tax return to the CRA. Most resident companies file a T2 every year, even if they had no activity.
Insider tip: Put registry and tax reminders in separate calendar entries. The T2 filing date is not the payment date, so set a reminder for each.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: A founder has a certificate but no ownership records. What should happen next? A. Assume the certificate proves their shares. · B. Complete company organisation and document share issuance. · C. Wait for the first tax bill.
items.text: The certificate confirms formation. The company must also organise and record ownership properly.

items.title: A new company receives its federal BN and income tax account. What should the founder do? A. Assume payroll is open. · B. Ignore tax accounts until sales begin. · C. Check whether other CRA program accounts are needed.
items.text: Federal incorporation provides the income tax account, but other program accounts depend on the company’s activities.

items.title: A company completes its annual registry return. What does that mean for its T2? A. The separate tax filing still needs attention. · B. The T2 is automatically filed. · C. There is no tax filing if the company is inactive.
items.text: A registry return updates company information. It does not replace the CRA’s corporate tax return.

items.title: Written response: Name two items for your startup folder and explain what each helps you check.
items.text: Filed articles help check the company structure; a banking confirmation helps check which account receives company payments.

blocks.text: A corporation needs a clear start after filing. Keep ownership records, company money and ongoing deadlines organised from the beginning.
Make a folder with the sections from the walkthrough. Put one document or a short task note in each section, then circle the task you will do next. Use your answers below as your plan.

items.title: Corporation
items.text: A company that is a legal person, separate from its owners.

items.title: Shareholder
items.text: Someone who owns shares in a company.

items.title: Director
items.text: A person who oversees the company.

items.title: Officer
items.text: A person named to run the daily work of the company.

items.title: Articles
items.text: The filing that sets out how the company is built.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: A company decision that is written down and approved.
